claim: Larval zebrafish combines position and velocity perception to construct a future positional estimate of its prey.
source: Using a novel naturalistic 3D setup, we show that the zebrafish combines position and velocity perception to construct a future positional estimate of its prey, indicating an ability to project trajectories forward in time.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the 3D behavioral setup showing that zebrafish use both position and velocity information during prey capture, as detailed in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Stochasticity in the fish's sensorimotor transformations provides a considerable advantage over equivalent noise-free strategies.
source: Importantly, the stochasticity in the fish's sensorimotor transformations provides a considerable advantage over equivalent noise-free strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data in Figure 6 showing that stochastic algorithms outperform deterministic ones in prey capture speed.

claim: Zebrafish are equipped with a recursive prey capture algorithm built up from simple stochastic rules.
source: In sum, our study reveals that zebrafish are equipped with a recursive prey capture algorithm, built up from simple stochastic rules, that embodies an implicit predictive model of the world.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing recursive halving of prey coordinates (Figure 5) and stochastic transformations (Figure 6), combined with computational modeling.

claim: Seemingly complicated behaviors like schooling in fish arise from stereotypic visuomotor rules being executed by members of the group.
source: For example, seemingly complicated behaviors like schooling in fish arise from stereotypic visuomotor rules being executed by members of the group, without reference to the emerging global pattern (Couzin and Krause, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Couzin and Krause, 2003.

claim: Bees learning to pull strings for hidden rewards are instituting a set of observational and associative learning rules in sequence.
source: Bees learning to pull strings for hidden rewards appear to be displaying insight and ingenuity, but are in fact instituting a set of observational and associative learning rules in sequence (Alem et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Alem et al., 2016.

claim: Humans and animals have evolved internal models that allow prediction of ongoing dynamics in the environment.
source: Indeed, humans and animals have evolved internal models that allow us to both predict ongoing dynamics in the environment and anticipate how our own actions give rise to consequences in the world (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Baillargeon, 1987; Mischiati et al., 2015; Borghuis and Leonardo, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Crayfish and paddlefish take advantage of stochastic resonance to detect sparse prey and predators.
source: Crayfish and paddlefish, for instance, both take advantage of stochastic resonance to detect sparse prey and predators (Douglass et al., 1993; Russett et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Douglass et al., 1993 and Russett et al., 1999.

claim: The larval zebrafish is a teleost with approximately 100,000 neurons.
source: The larval zebrafish, a teleost with ~100,000 neurons, is a tractable model organism amenable to an array of modern neuroscience techniques (Avella et al., 2012; Dunn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge about zebrafish neurobiology.

claim: Stabilization of position in turbulent streams by zebrafish is accomplished by instantiating a curl-detector for local water flow and an optomotor response.
source: For example, stabilization of position in turbulent streams is accomplished by instantiating a curl-detector for local water flow and an optomotor response (Oteiza et al., 2017; Naumann et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Oteiza et al., 2017 and Naumann et al., 2016.

claim: Energy-efficient foraging in zebrafish emerges from the fish's innate tendency to locomote via alternating series of unidirectional turns.
source: while energy-efficient foraging emerges from the zebrafish's innate tendency to locomote via alternating series of unidirectional turns (Dunn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Dunn et al., 2016.

claim: The zebrafish's ongoing behavior is largely probabilistic, reflecting the stochasticity of its neural systems.
source: Finally, the zebrafish's ongoing behavior is largely probabilistic, reflecting the stochasticity of its neural systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and general knowledge about zebrafish behavior.

claim: The precise number of unidirectional turns in any spontaneous swimming stretch by zebrafish is stochastic.
source: For instance, the precise number of unidirectional turns in any spontaneous swimming stretch is stochastic, while turn magnitude in response to angular optic flow varies widely (Dunn et al., 2016; Naumann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Dunn et al., 2016 and Naumann et al., 2016.

claim: Hunting sequences were recorded from 46 larval zebrafish using a behavioral setup that could simultaneously image the fish and its prey from the top and side at high resolution and speed.
source: Hunting sequences were recorded from 46 larval zebrafish using a behavioral setup that could simultaneously image the fish and its prey from the top and side at high resolution and speed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and is supported by the description in the text and Figure 1A showing the setup.

claim: Custom computer vision software was designed to reconstruct the fish's 3D position and two of the principal axes, yaw and pitch.
source: Custom computer vision software was designed to reconstruct the fish's 3D position and two of the principal axes, yaw and pitch (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods developed for the study, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Each paramecium is assigned an azimuth, altitude and distance as a positional coordinate, along with angular and radial velocities with respect to the fish's 3D point of view.
source: Hereby, each paramecium is assigned an azimuth, altitude and distance as a positional coordinate ('Prey Az, Prey Alt, Prey Dist'), along with angular (Prey δAz / δt, Prey δAlt / δt) and radial (Prey δDist / δt) velocities with respect to the fish's 3D point of view (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim describes the coordinate system used in the study, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Larval zebrafish swim in discrete 'bouts', which consist of a pulse of velocity lasting approximately 200 ms, followed by a variable period of intermittent quiescence.
source: Larval zebrafish swim in discrete 'bouts', which consist of a pulse of velocity lasting ~200 ms, followed by a variable period of intermittent quiescence (Figure 2A; Budick and O'Malley, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by both the current study's data (Figure 2A) and citation to prior work by Budick and O'Malley, 2000.

claim: Eye convergence allows the use of stereovision by creating a small binocular zone and is a well-known correlate of hunting state entrance in zebrafish.
source: Eye convergence, which allows the use of stereovision by creating a small binocular zone, is a well-known correlate of hunting state entrance in zebrafish (Gahtan et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Gahtan et al., 2005 and Bianco et al., 2011.

claim: The average hunting sequence ending in a strike lasted for five bouts with an interquartile range of 4 to 7.
source: The average hunting sequence ending in a strike in our dataset lasted for five bouts (Interquartile Range = 4 to 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: Fish almost invariably chose the closest paramecium in the environment conditioned on the fact that the paramecium was fairly close to its midline in azimuth and significantly above it in altitude.
source: Fish almost invariably chose the closest paramecium in the environment conditioned on the fact that the paramecium was fairly close to its midline in azimuth and significantly above it in altitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; μaz = 0.7° σaz = 48.4°; μalt = 19.9° σalt = 19.7°; μdist = 3.4 mm σdist = 1.6 mm).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strike zone is directly in front of and considerably above the fish with average coordinates of 0.9° Prey Az, 17.4° Prey Alt, 0.870 mm Prey Dist.
source: Pursuit bouts are conducted until prey are positioned in a 'strike zone', which defines the termination condition for successful hunts in spherical coordinates relative to the fish: this zone is directly in front of, and considerably above the fish (Figure 2B; avg. 0.9° Prey Az, 17.4° Prey Alt, .870 mm Prey Dist; Mearns et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Mearns et al., 2019.

claim: Bout Az and Bout ΔYaw are well correlated to Prey Az, with negligible offset (0.3° and 0.48°).
source: Regression fits show that Bout Az and Bout ΔYaw are well correlated to Prey Az, with negligible offset (0.3° and 0.48°).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the experimental data.

claim: A linear relationship exists between Bout Alt and Bout ΔPitch to Prey Alt with significant negative offsets (−15.13° and −1.79°).
source: A similar linear relationship is seen when mapping Bout Alt and Bout ΔPitch of pursuit bouts to Prey Alt, but this time with significant negative offsets (−15.13° and −1.79°).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the experimental data.

claim: 74% of prey in the assay have 3D vector velocity greater than 3 paramecium lengths per second.
source: Fish must capture prey that can move very quickly (in our assay, 74% 3D vector velocity >3 paramecium lengths per second, 27% > 6 paramecium lengths per second; avg. Prey δAz / δt = 29°/s, Prey δAlt / δt = 25°/s; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Every movement the fish performs during prey capture is strongly and proportionally influenced by both the radial and angular velocity of its prey.
source: We find that every movement the fish performs during prey capture is strongly and proportionally influenced by both the radial and angular velocity of its prey (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: All angular bout variables are amplified if prey are moving away from the fish and dampened when prey are moving towards the fish.
source: All angular bout variables are amplified if prey are moving away from the fish (Figure 3 light colors) and dampened when prey are moving towards the fish (Figure 3 dark colors; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Zebrafish transform projected prey position changes by 1.43 for Bout Az, 0.31 for Bout ΔYaw, 1.70 for Bout Alt, and 0.18 for Bout ΔPitch.
source: We find that zebrafish transform projected prey position changes by 1.43 for Bout Az,. 31 for Bout ΔYaw, 1.70 for Bout Alt, and. 18 for Bout ΔPitch (see Figure 3 legend).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations based on velocity coefficients from regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The linear relationship between Bout Distance and Prey Distance is only strong when prey are less than 4 mm from the fish.
source: The linear relationship between Bout Distance and Prey Distance, in general, is only strong when prey are <4 mm from the fish (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bout Distance is significantly modulated by radial prey velocity when prey are within 2 mm.
source: Bout Distance is significantly modulated by radial prey velocity (δDist / δt; see Figure 1D) when prey are within 2 mm (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 69% of pursuit bouts occur when prey are 0–2 mm from the fish.
source: Importantly, 69% of pursuit bouts occur when prey are 0–2 mm from the fish, indicating that Bout Distance is typically modulated by radial prey velocity
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: The velocity-based regression Model 3 improves hunting success over the position-only regression Model 2 by 65%.
source: The first clear result is that the velocity-based regression Model 3 (Green) improves hunting success over the position-only regression Model 2 (Orange) by 65%.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing different models in the virtual prey capture environment.

claim: The average number of bouts for the velocity-based model is one less than the position-only model, matching the average of the real fish.
source: Moreover, the average number of bouts is one less for the velocity model, matching the average of the real fish (Blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Model 6, which accounts for prey velocity and chooses ideally, improves success rate over the Real Fish model and Ideal Position model by 14% and 17%.
source: Model 6 (Gold), however, by accounting for prey velocity and choosing ideally, improves success rate over Model 1 (Real Fish) and 5 (Ideal Position) by 14% and 17%, reduces the average number of required bouts by 1
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing different models.

claim: Model 6 expends the most energy of any model per hunt sequence.
source: Nevertheless, Model 6 expends the most energy of any model per hunt sequence, meaning that fully ideal choice comes at an energetic cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Larval zebrafish reduce Prey Az and Prey Alt by a factor of 0.5 at each bout.
source: We find that larval zebrafish use neither of the two, but rather reduce Prey Az and Prey Alt by a factor of 0.5 at each bout.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When prey are below the fish, the slope changes to 0.9, meaning that the fish is only getting 10% closer in altitude per bout.
source: Notably, when prey are below the fish, the slope changes to 0.9, meaning that the fish is only getting 10% closer in altitude per bout.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: 92.4% of all bouts in the dataset occur when prey are above 0° Alt.
source: In fact, 92.4% of all bouts in our dataset occur when prey are above 0° Alt (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fish become 16% closer to the prey per bout on average, or in other words, the Prey Distance is scaled by 0.84 at every iteration.
source: We find that on average fish become 16% closer to the prey per bout, or in other words, the Prey Distance is scaled by 0.84 at every iteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: There is a clear graded increase in variance of the post-bout coordinate in all spherical planes as pre-bout coordinates trended away from the strike zone.
source: Interestingly, we noticed a clear graded increase in variance of the post-bout coordinate in all spherical planes as pre-bout coordinates trended away from the strike zone (Figure 5A, Figure 6A left panels, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figures 5A, 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The stochastic model outperformed the deterministic model in terms of capture speed.
source: Remarkably, the stochastic model outperformed the deterministic model in terms of capture speed (# Bouts to Capture, Figure 6B; Wilcoxon signed rank = 7.5 * 10−17).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B with statistical testing.

claim: Injecting proportional noise into deterministic bout choices speeds up prey capture.
source: To confirm that graded stochasticity in our Bayesian model was responsible for its increased prey capture speed, we simply injected proportional noise into deterministic bout choices and asked whether we could speed up prey capture (Figure 6C,D). This was clearly the case (Wilcoxon Signed Rank: 1.87 * 10−9 azimuth, 3.96 * 10−14 distance)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6C,D with statistical testing.

claim: The average performance when injecting proportional noise is typically equivalent or better by one bout compared to deterministic choices.
source: Nevertheless, the average performance when injecting proportional noise is typically equivalent or better by one bout (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Improving by one bout constitutes an average 14–25% gain in capture speed given that successful hunts had an interquartile range of 4 to 7 total bouts.
source: Given that successful hunts in our dataset had an interquartile range of 4 to 7 total bouts, improving by one bout constitutes an average 14–25% gain in capture speed.
evidence: This claim is based on calculation from the data on hunt bout numbers.

claim: Speed sensitive neurons that discriminate between 'fast' and 'slow' prey-like stimuli have been uncovered in the zebrafish optic tectum.
source: Speed sensitive neurons that discriminate between 'fast' and 'slow' prey-like stimuli have been uncovered in the zebrafish optic tectum (Bianco and Engert, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Bianco and Engert, 2015.

claim: 'Small field' tectal neurons that respond to velocity have been found in toads.
source: while 'small field' tectal neurons that respond to velocity have been found in toads (Ewert, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Ewert, 1987.

claim: Velocity perception is used to point-estimate a future prey position, and the fish conducts bouts to achieve this estimate by biasing their prey position-controlled movements.
source: Unlike these and other reports studying velocity during prey capture (Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Patterson et al., 2013; Monroy and Nishikawa, 2011), we specifically contend that velocity perception is used to point-estimate a future prey position, and that the fish conducts bouts to achieve this estimate, on average, by biasing their prey position-controlled movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data analysis and represents an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Without velocity perception, the azimuth and altitude coordinates of prey after bouts are less likely to lie near the strike zone.
source: We show that the perception and projection of velocity is key to prey capture success, and that without it, the azimuth and altitude coordinates of prey after bouts are less likely to lie near the strike zone (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Monkeys predict future locations of virtual prey using Newtonian physical attributes, and these attributes are reflected by neural activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate.
source: Relatedly, monkeys also predict future locations of virtual prey using Newtonian physical attributes in a very similar paradigm to that shown here. In the monkey brain, these attributes are all reflected by neural activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate, which has no known homolog in the zebrafish, nor in other simple animals that use predictive prey models (Yoo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Yoo et al., 2019.

claim: The amount of 'fixed noise' in the fish's azimuth transformations is 7.64°, which is the standard deviation of Post-Bout Prey Az given a Pre-Bout Prey Az coordinate of 0°.
source: Specifically, interesting relationships in the data we provide suggest that the fish's algorithms are built around the capabilities and constraints of its body. First, the amount of 'fixed noise' in the fish's azimuth transformations is 7.64°. This is the standard deviation of Post-Bout Prey Az given a Pre-Bout Prey Az coordinate of 0°, the minimum of graded stochasticity observed in Figure 6A.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The standard deviation of the strike zone is 7.2° in azimuth.
source: The standard deviation of the strike zone itself is 7.2° in azimuth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: The fish's strike zone is constructed to deal with noise that the fish cannot overcome in its motor program.
source: We contend that the similarity between these two numbers suggests that the fish's strike zone is constructed to deal with noise that the fish cannot overcome in its motor program.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the similarity between fixed noise and strike zone variance.

claim: The fish's algorithm for transforming prey altitude biases the prey to approximately 18° above the fish, which aligns almost perfectly with the mean altitude coordinate at which they strike (17.4°).
source: Further evidence for embodied knowledge comes from the bias in the fish's responses to prey altitude. The fish's algorithm for transforming prey altitude biases the prey to ~18° above the fish, which aligns almost perfectly with the mean altitude coordinate at which they strike (17.4°, Figures 2, 3 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: To open its jaw widely for paramecium entrance into the mouth, the fish must tilt its head up due to torsional constraints.
source: The mechanics of the fish jaw necessitate this: to open its jaw widely for paramecium entrance into the mouth, the fish must tilt its head up due to torsional constraints (Mearns et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Mearns et al., 2019.

claim: Graded variance is minimal for altitude transformations at Pre-Bout Alt = 20°, whereas the azimuth minimum is at 0°.
source: Also of note is that graded variance is minimal for altitude transformations at Pre-Bout Alt = 20° (Figure 6A), whereas the azimuth minimum is at 0°
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Experiments were conducted according to the guidelines of the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the Standing Committee on the Use of Animals in Research of Harvard University.
source: Experiments were conducted according to the guidelines of the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the Standing Committee on the Use of Animals in Research of Harvard University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance for the study.

claim: All experiments were performed on dpf 7–8 larval zebrafish of the WIK strain.
source: All experiments were performed on dpf 7–8 larval zebrafish of the WIK strain.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Fish were raised in an automated system where they were delivered paramecia twice a day from dpf4 onward.
source: Fish were raised in an automated system where they were delivered paramecia twice a day from dpf4 onward.
evidence: This describes the rearing conditions for the experimental subjects.

claim: Fish were fasted for 4–6 hr before experiments.
source: Fish were fasted for 4–6 hr before experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: 3.56 megapixel images were simultaneously acquired from the top and side of the tank using two Point Grey Grasshopper 3 NIR cameras synchronized at 62.5 Hz.
source: 3.56 megapixel images were simultaneously acquired from the top and side of the tank using two Point Grey Grasshopper 3 NIR cameras; the cameras were synchronized by a TTL pulse triggered by a Pyboard microcontroller at 62.5 Hz.
evidence: This describes the imaging methodology used in the study.

claim: Camera positions were calibrated using known reference points with approximately 200 micron mean error.
source: Camera positions were calibrated by using known reference points (i.e. body features of the fish) for the shared plane of the cameras. Identification of known object positions in both planes was extremely accurate (~200 micron mean error)
evidence: This describes the calibration accuracy of the imaging system.

claim: Fish hunted in the white light illuminated condition for 8 min before the experiment was terminated.
source: Fish hunted in the white light illuminated condition for 8 min before the experiment was terminated.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Fish that did not consume more than one paramecium over the 8 min experiment were discarded for analysis (46/53 fish passed this criteria).
source: Fish that did not consume more than one paramecium over the 8 min experiment were discarded for analysis (46/53 fish passed this criteria).
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for data analysis.

claim: Pitch was calculated by taking the 2D vertical angle in the side camera and fitting a cone to the fish using the yaw angle from the top camera.
source: Pitch was calculated by taking the 2D vertical angle in the side camera and fitting a cone to the fish using the yaw angle from the top camera.
evidence: This describes the computational method for calculating pitch.

claim: Dirichlet Process Mixture Models can approximate a broad class of multivariate distributions without requiring a priori specification of the number of components in the mixture model.
source: DPMMs can approximate a broad class of multivariate distributions without requiring a priori specification of the number of components in the mixture model.
evidence: This describes a property of the statistical modeling approach used.

claim: The implicit predictive model of 3D prey motion is embodied by the fish's stochastic recursive algorithm, shaped by the constraints and capabilities of the fish, and formulated by the interaction of three simple rules.
source: All things considered, the implicit predictive model of 3D prey motion shown in this study is: 1) embodied by the fish's stochastic recursive algorithm 2) shaped by the constraints and capabilities of the fish and 3) formulated by the interaction of three simple rules.
evidence: This is a summary claim synthesizing the main findings of the study.

claim: The three simple rules transform position of prey into fish movements, bias the vigor of fish movements based on prey velocity, and inject proportional noise into each sensorimotor transformation.
source: These rules transform position of prey into fish movements, bias the vigor of fish movements based on prey velocity, and inject proportional noise into each sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: This summarizes the three main rules identified in the study.
